step2_cannibalisation.evidence: content/equipment/pump-not-priming.mdx (EQP-001) contains 38 air-leak-related mentions. Its entire five-step 'Check in this order' IS the suction-side air-leak procedure: water level and valves; pump lid, o-ring and basket; suction lines, unions and diverter valve; impeller and skimmer blockage; check valve. It already covers bubbles in the lid window as the diagnostic signal, diverter valve stem seals, and escalation to pressure testing. It already cites a source on testing for suction-side air leaks.

AGREED_BOUNDARY.EQP-001 owns: The pump that will not prime or loses prime, and the complete procedure for FINDING and FIXING a suction-side air leak.
AGREED_BOUNDARY.EQP-005 owns: The pump that primes and runs normally and still pushes bubbles into the pool. Its job is IDENTIFICATION — deciding whether those bubbles are a leak at all — and then routing to EQP-001 for the leak hunt.
AGREED_BOUNDARY.hardRule: EQP-005 must NOT reproduce the five-step leak procedure. One line and a link. If the draft starts explaining how to test the lid o-ring, the boundary has failed.

otherAdjacencies.note: lists 'air leak in suction line' as one of four low-pressure causes and already links to EQP-001. Cross-link both ways; EQP-004 owns the flow framing, EQP-005 owns the bubbles framing.

step3_serpGap.whoRanks: swimuniversity, poolresearch, Orenda's ask site, mavaquadoc, minibuckettest (two separate posts), poolmarvel.
step3_serpGap.whatTheyAllDo: Uniform: bubbles mean a suction-side air leak, here is the list of places to check. Every page is a shorter, worse version of what EQP-001 already does.
step3_serpGap.THE_GAP: None of them separate the two situations that matter. Bubbles from a pump that WILL NOT PRIME is a leak hunt. Bubbles from a pump that primes and runs fine is a different, shorter list — and one branch of it is a salt cell, which most of these pages either ignore or wave away as harmless.
step3_serpGap.theInversion: The reassuring line found on forums and several of these pages — 'if you have a salt system, small bubbles are normal, ignore them' — is NOT supported by manufacturer literature. See the mechanism below. This is the article's reason to exist and it points the opposite way to the consensus.

step3_mechanism.claim: The standard reassurance — 'you have a salt system, bubbles are normal' — is not backed by manufacturer literature, and the one thing the manufacturers DO document about gas from a salt cell is a hazard warning tied to low flow.
sourcedFacts: Pentair IntelliChlor installation and user's guide, verbatim: 'WARNING: Never operate the IntelliChlor Salt Chlorine Generator (SCG) without proper flow or water circulation. A build-up of flammable gases will result in hazardous conditions.'

Same manual, verbatim: 'WARNING: CHLORINE GAS BUILDUP CAN OCCUR WITH IMPROPER WIRING: ... the Power Center must be installed on and wired to the load side of the time clock, electronically controlled switch, or relay load side, so that it will receive power only when the pool pump is on. Otherwise, dangerous chlorine gas buildup can occur.'

Hayward AquaRite manual documents the flow switch as the protective interlock: 'When illuminated, the flow switch has detected no water flowing and the Aqua Rite has stopped generating chlorine.' It also specifies at least a 12 inch (25 cm) straight pipe run upstream of the flow switch.

theNegativeFinding.detail: NEITHER the Hayward AquaRite manual NOR the Pentair IntelliChlor manual describes visible bubbling at the returns as normal or expected during chlorine generation. Searched both directly. No such statement exists in either.
theNegativeFinding.handling: Write this as an explicit unknown, house style. Do NOT assert 'salt cells make harmless bubbles' — that claim is everywhere online and is unsourced. What can be said: gas generation at the cell is real and manufacturers treat it seriously enough to warn about it, but no manufacturer documentation was found stating that visible bubbles at the return are a normal operating condition.

step3_mechanism.whyItMatters: It flips the usual advice at exactly the point where it's dangerous. The moment a reader concludes 'salt cell, therefore fine,' they stop investigating — and bubbles frequently co-occur with poor flow, which is the precise condition Pentair warns produces a build-up of flammable gases. The safe reading is the reverse: bubbles plus a salt system means check that flow is genuinely adequate and the flow switch is working, not that there's nothing to look at.

safetyRequirements: §10 safety block required: flammable gas build-up warning is a manufacturer safety statement and must not be softened.
The improper-wiring warning is genuinely useful and rarely repeated — a salt cell powered independently of the pump can generate with no flow. Worth its own callout.
